questions.question: You must prove: "For every integer n, if n is a multiple of 6, then n is even." What should the first two lines of your proof be?
options: Let n = 6. Then n is even.
Assume n is even. Show n is a multiple of 6.
Let n be an arbitrary integer. Assume n is a multiple of 6.
Assume, for contradiction, that every integer is odd.
questions.explanation: The claim starts with "for all", so you introduce an arbitrary n. Then it is an implication, so you assume the if-part. Choosing n = 6 proves only one case, and assuming n is even sets up the converse instead.

questions.question: In the proof that √2 is irrational, which assumption makes the contradiction possible?
options: That a and b are both odd
That a/b is written in lowest terms
questions.explanation: The proof shows that a and b must both be even. That conflicts only with the assumption that the fraction has no common factor. Any fraction can be reduced first, so this assumption costs nothing.

questions.question: Why does the L-tromino proof need to handle EVERY position of the missing cell in its inductive hypothesis?
options: Because after the centre L is placed, each quadrant's missing cell can be anywhere in it
Because the base case is a 1 by 1 board
Because induction always needs two base cases
Because the number of pieces must be a multiple of 3
questions.explanation: The original hole could be in any position within its quadrant, and the other three quadrants get their hole at a corner. To recurse, P(n) must cover any single missing cell. A weaker hypothesis would not apply to all four quadrants.

questions.question: A student "proves" n = n + 1 for all n by showing: if n = n + 1, then adding 1 to both sides gives n + 1 = n + 2. What is wrong?
options: The inductive step is invalid algebra
There is no true base case, so the chain never starts
questions.explanation: The step itself is valid: if P(n) were true, P(n + 1) would follow. But P(0), which says 0 = 1, is false. Without a true base case, induction proves nothing.
